danish.title: Tolvte bog (1812) — Kapitel 7
paragraphs: Den forfærdelige nyhed om Borodinó-slaget, om tabene i dræbte og sårede, og den endnu mere forfærdelige nyhed om Moskvas tab nåede Vorónezj midt i september. Prinsesse Marja, der kun gennem tidsskriftet havde erfaret om sin broders sår og ikke havde nogen sikker besked om ham, forberedte sig (som Nikolaj hørte, for han havde ikke selv set hende igen) på at tage af sted for at søge efter fyrst Andrej.

Da Nikolaj modtog nyheden om Borodinó-slaget og Moskvas opgivelse, blev han ikke grebet af fortvivlelse, vrede, hævnlyst eller nogen følelse af den art, men alt i Vorónezj syntes ham pludselig kedeligt og trættende, og han oplevede en ubestemt følelse af skam og pinlighed. De samtaler, han hørte, forekom ham uoprigtige; han vidste ikke, hvordan han skulle bedømme alle disse anliggender, og følte, at kun i regimentet ville alt atter blive klart for ham. Han skyndte sig med at afslutte hestekøbene og blev ofte urimeligt vred på sin tjener og skvadronens kvartermester.

Få dage før hans afrejse blev der holdt en særlig takkegudstjeneste i domkirken for den russiske sejr, som Nikolaj overværede. Han stod lidt bag guvernøren og holdt sig i militær holdning gennem gudstjenesten, mens han tænkte på en stor mangfoldighed af emner. Da gudstjenesten var overstået, vinkede guvernørens kone ham til sig.
»Har De set prinsessen?« spurgte hun og indikerede med en hovedbevægelse en dame, der stod på den modsatte side, hinsides koret.

Nikolaj genkendte straks prinsesse Marja, ikke så meget på profilen, han så under hendes hat, som på den følelse af omsorg, skyhed og medlidenhed, der øjeblikkeligt greb ham. Prinsesse Marja, tydeligvis fordybet i sine tanker, korsede sig for sidste gang, inden hun forlod kirken.

Nikolaj så på hendes ansigt med overraskelse. Det var det samme ansigt, han havde set før, det samme generelle udtryk af forfinet, indre, åndeligt arbejde, men nu var det helt anderledes oplyst. Der var et rørende udtryk af sorg, bøn og håb i det. Som det tidligere var sket i hendes nærvær, gik Nikolaj hen til hende uden at vente på guvernørens kones tilskyndelse og uden at spørge sig selv, om det var rigtigt og passende at henvende sig til hende her i kirken, og fortalte hende, at han havde hørt om hendes sorg og følte med af hele sit hjerte. Så snart hun hørte hans stemme, tændtes en levende glød i hendes ansigt, der oplyste både hendes sorg og hendes glæde.

»Der er én ting, jeg gerne ville sige Dem, prinsesse,« sagde Rostov. »Hvis Deres bror, fyrst Andrej Nikolajevitj, ikke var i live, ville det straks være blevet meddelt i tidsskriftet, da han er oberst.«
Prinsessen så på ham uden at forstå, hvad han sagde, men opmuntret af udtrykket af deltagende medfølelse i hans ansigt.

»Og jeg har kendt så mange tilfælde, hvor et granatsplintesår« (tidsskriftet sagde, det var en granat) »enten straks er dødeligt eller ganske let,« fortsatte Nikolaj. »Vi må håbe det bedste, og jeg er sikker på...«
Prinsesse Marja afbrød ham.

»Åh, det ville være så forfærde...« begyndte hun, og forhindret af bevægelse i at fuldføre sætningen, bøjede hun hovedet med en bevægelse, der var lige så yndefuld som alt andet, hun gjorde i hans nærvær, og gik med et taknemmeligt blik hen mod udgangen, fulgt af sin tante.

Den aften gik Nikolaj ikke ud, men blev hjemme for at ordne nogle mellemværender med hestehandlerne. Da han var færdig med det, var det allerede for sent at gå nogen steder hen, men stadig for tidligt at gå i seng, og han vandrede længe op og ned i værelset og grublede over sit liv, noget han sjældent gjorde.

Prinsesse Marja havde gjort et behageligt indtryk på ham, da han mødte hende i Smolénsk-provinsen. At han havde truffet hende under så usædvanlige omstændigheder, og at hans moder engang havde nævnt hende som et godt parti, havde draget hans særlige opmærksomhed mod hende. Da han mødte hende igen i Vorónezj, var det indtryk, hun gjorde, ikke blot behageligt men stærkt. Nikolaj var slået af den særlige moralske skønhed, han iagttog hos hende på dette tidspunkt. Han var imidlertid ved at forberede sig på at rejse, og det var ikke faldet ham ind at beklage, at han derved berøvede sig muligheder for at møde hende. Men denne dags møde i kirken havde, følte han, gjort et dybere indtryk end ønskeligt for hans sjælefred. Det blege, triste, forfinede ansigt, det strålende blik, de blide, yndefulde bevægelser og frem for alt den dybe og ømme sorg, der udtrykte sig i alle hendes træk, rørte ham og vakte hans medfølelse. Hos mænd kunne Rostov ikke udholde at se udtrykket for et højere åndeligt liv (derfor holdt han ikke af fyrst Andrej) og betegnede det foragteligt som filosofi og drømmeri, men hos prinsesse Marja var det netop den sorg, der afslørede dybden af en hel åndelig verden, der var ham fremmed, der udøvede en uimodståelig tiltrækning.

»Hun må være en vidunderlig kvinde. En sand engel!« sagde han til sig selv. »Hvorfor er jeg ikke fri? Hvorfor havde jeg så travlt med Sonja?« Og han sammenlignede uvilkårligt de to: manglen på åndelighed hos den ene og rigdommen af den hos den anden — en åndelighed, han selv manglede og derfor satte allerhøjest pris på. Han forsøgte at forestille sig, hvad der ville ske, hvis han var fri. Hvordan han ville fri til hende, og hvordan hun ville blive hans hustru. Men nej, han kunne ikke forestille sig det. Han følte ærefrygt, og intet klart billede viste sig for hans sind. Han havde for længe siden forestillet sig en fremtid med Sonja, og det var alt klart og enkelt, netop fordi det hele var gennemtænkt, og han kendte alt i Sonja, men det var umuligt at forestille sig en fremtid med prinsesse Marja, fordi han ikke forstod hende men simpelthen elskede hende.
Dagdrømmene om Sonja havde haft noget muntert og legende over sig, men at drømme om prinsesse Marja var altid svært og en smule skræmmende.

»Hvor hun bad!« tænkte han. »Man kunne se, at hele hendes sjæl var i bønnen. Ja, det var den bøn, der kan flytte bjerge, og jeg er sikker på, at hendes bøn vil blive hørt. Hvorfor beder jeg ikke om det, jeg ønsker?« tænkte han pludselig. »Hvad ønsker jeg? At være fri, løst fra Sonja... Hun havde ret,« tænkte han og mindedes, hvad guvernørens kone havde sagt: »Intet andet end ulykke kan komme af at gifte sig med Sonja. Rodet, sorg for Mamma... økonomiske vanskeligheder... rod, forfærdeligt rod! Desuden elsker jeg hende ikke — ikke som jeg burde. Åh, Gud! Befri mig fra denne forfærdelige, uløselige stilling!« begyndte han pludselig at bede. »Ja, bøn kan flytte bjerge, men man må have tro og ikke bede, som Natasja og jeg gjorde som børn, om at sneen skulle blive til sukker — og så løbe ud i gården for at se, om det var sket. Nej, men jeg beder ikke om bagateller nu,« tænkte han, mens han lagde sin pibe i et hjørne, og med foldede hænder stillede sig foran ikonet. Blødgjort af minderne om prinsesse Marja begyndte han at bede, som han ikke havde gjort i lang tid. Der stod tårer i hans øjne og i hans hals, da døren blev åbnet og Lavrúsjka kom ind med nogle papirer.
»Klodrian! Hvorfor kommer du ind uden at blive kaldt?« råbte Nikolaj og skiftede hurtigt holdning.
»Fra guvernøren,« sagde Lavrúsjka med søvnig stemme. »En kurer er ankommet, og der er et brev til Dem.«
»Nå godt, tak. Du kan gå!«

Nikolaj tog de to breve, hvoraf det ene var fra hans moder og det andet fra Sonja. Han genkendte dem på håndskriften og åbnede Sonjas først. Han havde kun læst nogle få linjer, da han blev bleg, og hans øjne åbnede sig vidt af frygt og glæde.
»Nej, det er ikke muligt!« udbrød han højt.

Ude af stand til at sidde stille gik han op og ned i værelset med brevet og læste det. Han skimmede det, læste det igen og endnu engang, og midt i værelset løftede han skuldrene, bredte armene ud, med munden vidt åben og øjnene stirrende. Det, han netop med tillid havde bedt Gud om, var sket; men Nikolaj var lige så forbavset, som om det var noget ekstraordinært og uventet, og som om selve den omstændighed, at det var sket så hurtigt, beviste, at det ikke kom fra Gud, som han havde bedt til, men ved et almindeligt tilfælde.

Dette uventede og, som det syntes Nikolaj, helt frivillige brev fra Sonja befriede ham fra den knude, der havde bundet ham, og som der ikke syntes at være nogen udvej af. Hun skrev, at de seneste ulykkelige begivenheder — tabet af næsten hele Rostov-familiens Moskva-ejendom — og grevindens gentagne ønske om, at Nikolaj skulle gifte sig med prinsesse Bolkonskaja, sammen med hans tavshed og kulde i den seneste tid, alt dette tilsammen havde fået hende til at beslutte at løse ham fra hans løfte og give ham fuldstændig frihed.

Det ville være mig for smertefuldt at tænke, at jeg kunne være årsag til sorg eller splid i den familie, der har været så god mod mig (skrev hun), og min kærlighed har intet andet mål end de menneskers lykke, jeg elsker; derfor, Nikolaj, beder jeg Dem betragte Dem selv som fri og være forvisset om, at uanset hvad, kan ingen elske Dem højere end Deres
Sonja

Begge breve var skrevet fra Tróitsa. Det andet, fra grevinden, beskrev deres sidste dage i Moskva, deres afrejse, branden og ødelæggelsen af al deres ejendom. I dette brev nævnte grevinden også, at fyrst Andrej var blandt de sårede, der rejste med dem; hans tilstand var meget kritisk, men lægen sagde, at der nu var mere håb. Sonja og Natasja plejede ham.

Næste dag tog Nikolaj sin moders brev med og gik for at besøge prinsesse Marja. Hverken han eller hun sagde et ord om, hvad »Natasja plejer ham« kunne betyde, men takket være dette brev blev Nikolaj pludselig næsten lige så fortrolig med prinsessen, som om de var beslægtede.
Den følgende dag fulgte han prinsesse Marja til vogns på hendes rejse til Jaroslávl, og et par dage senere rejste han selv for at slutte sig til sit regiment.

english.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: The dreadful news of the battle of Borodino reached Voronezh in the middle of September, with word of our killed and wounded and, worse still, of the loss of Moscow. Princess Mary had learned of her brother's wound only from the Gazette and had no definite news of him. She was getting ready (so Nicholas heard; he hadn't seen her again himself) to set off in search of Prince Andrew.

News of the battle of Borodino and the abandonment of Moscow did not throw Rostov into despair, anger, a thirst for vengeance or anything of the kind. Instead, everything in Voronezh suddenly struck him as dull and tiresome, and he felt a vague shame and awkwardness. The conversations he overheard seemed insincere. He didn't know how to judge all these events and felt that only in the regiment would things become clear to him again. He hurried to finish buying the horses, and kept losing his temper for no reason with his servant and the squadron quartermaster.

A few days before he left, a special thanksgiving service for the Russian victory was held in the cathedral, and Nicholas attended. He stood a little behind the governor and kept a properly military bearing through the service while his mind wandered over all sorts of subjects. When it ended, the governor's wife beckoned him over.
"Have you seen the princess?" she asked, nodding toward a lady who stood on the opposite side, beyond the choir.

Nicholas knew Princess Mary at once, less from the profile he could see under her bonnet than from the rush of concern, shyness and pity that came over him. Princess Mary, plainly lost in her thoughts, was crossing herself for the last time before leaving the church.

Nicholas looked at her face in surprise. It was the face he had seen before, with the same look of refined inner spiritual effort, yet now it was lit up quite differently. It showed a touching mixture of sorrow, prayer and hope. As had happened before when she was near, Nicholas went up to her without waiting for the governor's wife to prompt him, and without asking himself whether it was proper to speak to her here in church. He told her he had heard of her trouble and sympathized with his whole soul. The moment she heard his voice a bright glow came into her face, lighting up her sorrow and her joy together.
"There's one thing I wanted to tell you, Princess," said Rostov. "If your brother, Prince Andrew Nikolaevich, were no longer alive, the Gazette would have announced it at once, since he's a colonel."
The princess looked at him without grasping what he said, but she was cheered by the regretful sympathy in his face.

"And I've known so many cases of a splinter wound" (the Gazette said it was a shell) "that either killed the man at once or turned out to be very slight," Nicholas went on. "We must hope for the best, and I'm sure..."
Princess Mary cut him short.

"Oh, that would be so dread..." she began, but she was too agitated to finish. She bowed her head with a movement as graceful as everything she did in his presence, gave him a grateful look, and went out after her aunt.

That evening Nicholas didn't go out. He stayed home to settle some accounts with the horse dealers. When he finished, it was too late to go anywhere and still too early for bed, and for a long time he paced the room, thinking over his life, which he rarely did.

Princess Mary had made a pleasant impression on him when he met her in Smolensk province. He had come across her in such exceptional circumstances, and his mother had once mentioned her as a good match, so he had paid her particular attention. When he met her again in Voronezh, the impression was not merely pleasing but strong. He had been struck by the unusual moral beauty he saw in her then. Yet he was about to leave, and it hadn't occurred to him to regret that he was giving up chances of seeing her. But that day's meeting in church, he felt, had gone deeper than was good for his peace of mind. That pale, sad, refined face, that radiant look, those gentle graceful gestures, and above all the deep tender sorrow in every feature of her face stirred him and drew out his sympathy. In men, Rostov couldn't stand the sign of a higher spiritual life (that was why he disliked Prince Andrew), and he scornfully called it philosophy and dreaminess. But in Princess Mary, that very sorrow, which showed the depth of a whole spiritual world foreign to him, was an irresistible attraction.

"She must be a wonderful woman. A real angel!" he said to himself. "Why am I not free? Why did I rush into things with Sonya?" And he couldn't help comparing the two: the lack of spirituality in one and the abundance of it in the other, a spirituality he lacked himself and therefore valued most highly. He tried to picture what would happen if he were free: how he would propose to her and how she would become his wife. But no, he couldn't imagine it. He felt awed, and no clear picture came to his mind. Long ago he had pictured a future with Sonya, and it was all clear and simple just because it had been thought through and he knew everything there was to know about Sonya. But a future with Princess Mary was impossible to picture, because he didn't understand her; he simply loved her.
Daydreams about Sonya had had something merry and playful in them, but dreaming of Princess Mary was always difficult and a little frightening.

"How she prayed!" he thought. "You could see her whole soul was in her prayer. Yes, that's the prayer that moves mountains, and I'm sure hers will be answered. Why don't I pray for what I want?" he suddenly thought. "What do I want? To be free, to be released from Sonya... She was right," he thought, remembering what the governor's wife had said: "Nothing but misfortune can come of marrying Sonya. Muddles, grief for Mamma... business difficulties... muddles, terrible muddles! Besides, I don't love her, not as I should. Oh, God! Release me from this dreadful, inextricable position!" he suddenly began to pray. "Yes, prayer can move mountains, but you have to have faith. You can't pray the way Natasha and I did as children, asking that the snow turn into sugar and then running out into the yard to see whether it had. No, I'm not praying for trifles now," he thought, and he put his pipe down in a corner, folded his hands and stood in front of the icon. Softened by his memories of Princess Mary, he began to pray as he hadn't for a long time. There were tears in his eyes and in his throat when the door opened and Lavrushka came in with some papers.
"Blockhead! Why do you come in without being called?" cried Nicholas, quickly changing his pose.
"From the governor," said Lavrushka in a sleepy voice. "A courier has arrived, and there's a letter for you."
"Well, all right, thanks. You can go!"

Nicholas took the two letters, one from his mother and the other from Sonya. He knew them by the handwriting and opened Sonya's first. He had read only a few lines when he turned pale, and his eyes opened wide with fear and joy.
"No, it's not possible!" he cried aloud.

He couldn't sit still. He paced the room with the letter in his hand, reading it. He ran his eye over it, then read it again, and again, and then he stopped in the middle of the room, shrugged, spread out his hands, and stood with his mouth wide open and his eyes fixed. What he had just been praying for, confident that God would hear him, had come to pass. Yet Nicholas was as astonished as if it were something extraordinary and unexpected. It was as if the very speed with which it had happened proved that it hadn't come from the God he had prayed to, but from some ordinary coincidence.

This unexpected letter from Sonya, which seemed to Nicholas entirely of her own free will, freed him from the knot that bound him, from which there had seemed no escape. She wrote that the latest misfortunes, the loss of almost all the Rostovs' Moscow property, and the countess' repeated wish that Nicholas marry Princess Bolkonskaya, together with his silence and coldness of late, had all led her to decide to release him from his promise and set him completely free.

It would be too painful for me to think that I might cause sorrow or discord in the family that has been so good to me (she wrote), and my love has no aim but the happiness of those I love. So, Nicholas, I beg you to consider yourself free, and to be sure that, in spite of everything, no one can love you more than does
Your Sonya

Both letters were written from Troitsa. The other, from the countess, described their last days in Moscow, their departure, the fire and the destruction of all their property. In it the countess also mentioned that Prince Andrew was among the wounded traveling with them. His condition was very critical, but the doctor said there was now more hope. Sonya and Natasha were nursing him.

Next day Nicholas took his mother's letter and went to see Princess Mary. Neither of them said a word about what "Natasha nursing him" might mean, but thanks to this letter Nicholas suddenly became almost as close to the princess as if they were relations.
The following day he saw Princess Mary off on her journey to Yaroslavl, and a few days later he left to rejoin his regiment.
